examTypeMix: Written short-answer only, mirroring the mock exam paper which is policy- and management-focused with no multiple-choice, true/false, calculation, or pseudocode questions.

questions.question: Name two categories of IT infrastructure components, describe each category's role, and explain how the two categories connect to other infrastructure layers.
questions.expected: Example answer: Servers provide computing resources for applications, databases, and middleware. Storage provides persistent data capacity through local disks, SAN, NAS, or cloud storage. Servers connect to storage to read and write application and database data; both are linked through networking and are housed or managed through data-center or cloud infrastructure.

questions.question: Explain the role of applications and security in an IT infrastructure, including how they interact with other component categories.
questions.expected: Applications deliver business functionality to users and normally run on operating systems, virtual machines, servers, and databases. Security is a cross-cutting layer involving authentication, authorization, encryption, monitoring, and access control. Applications enforce security policies at the user and business-process level, while security controls also protect networks, operating systems, databases, and physical infrastructure.

questions.question: Compare on-premise, IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS in terms of what the customer manages.
questions.expected: In on-premise, the customer manages all layers: applications, security, databases, operating systems, virtualization, servers, storage, networking, and data centers. In IaaS, the provider manages the lower infrastructure layers, while the customer still manages applications, security, databases, and operating systems. In PaaS, the provider also manages databases and operating systems, leaving the customer mainly responsible for applications and security configuration. In SaaS, the provider manages almost everything, and the customer mainly configures and uses the application.

questions.question: A university wants a student scheduling system with fast deployment and minimal infrastructure responsibility, but it is worried about vendor lock-in. Which service model is most likely, and what trade-off should management recognize?
questions.expected: SaaS is most likely because the university wants fast deployment and minimal responsibility for infrastructure, updates, and scalability. The trade-off is reduced control and customization, plus dependency on the provider's availability, security posture, pricing, and future product direction. Vendor lock-in should be managed contractually and through data-export and integration requirements.

questions.question: Classify personal, workgroup, enterprise, and interorganizational information systems and give one example of each.
questions.expected: A personal information system supports one user, such as a personal note-taking or invoicing app. A workgroup information system supports a team, such as a shared project-management tool. An enterprise information system supports an entire organization, such as ERP or CRM. An interorganizational information system spans multiple organizations, such as EDI or a supply-chain integration platform.

questions.question: Use Leavitt's Diamond to explain why introducing a new information system can fail even when the technology works correctly.
questions.expected: Leavitt's Diamond argues that people, processes, technology, and organizational structure are interdependent. A technically working system can still fail if users are not trained, workflows are not redesigned, roles and reporting lines are unclear, or incentives conflict with the new process. Successful implementation requires adjusting all four dimensions rather than treating the system as only a technology change.

questions.question: Distinguish data, information, and knowledge using a business example.
questions.expected: Data are raw facts, such as sales numbers, dates, or product IDs. Information is data processed and presented in context, such as a report showing that sales increased in a particular region. Knowledge is understanding the relationship and implication, for example recognizing that the increase came from a new product line and deciding to invest more in that line.

questions.question: Name five characteristics of high-quality information and explain why two of them matter for management decisions.
questions.expected: High-quality information can be accessible, accurate, complete, economical, relevant, reliable, secure, timely, and verifiable. Accuracy matters because incorrect information can lead to wrong decisions even if the report looks professional. Timeliness matters because information that arrives after the decision window may no longer be useful.

questions.question: Explain why data governance is described as the core component of data management rather than just an IT task.
questions.expected: Data governance defines roles, responsibilities, standards, and processes for ensuring data can be trusted and used across the organization. It is not just an IT task because data quality, access rights, compliance, ownership, and business meaning require participation from organizational leadership and business units. IT can operate systems, but governance decides who is responsible for data and how data issues are prevented and corrected.

questions.question: Describe the main phases of data lifecycle management and explain the purpose of publishing data descriptions.
questions.expected: Data lifecycle management includes defining data needs, evaluating sources, acquiring data, storing data, publishing data descriptions, accessing and using data, evaluating data, and archiving or discarding it. Publishing data descriptions means creating metadata or catalog information so users know what data exists, what it means, where it comes from, and whether it is suitable for their purpose.

questions.question: A film festival expects 150000 attendees and more than 100 films. Explain why a DBMS is preferable to a spreadsheet for managing ticketing and attendance data.
questions.expected: A DBMS is preferable because the data volume, concurrent access, integrity requirements, and need for reliable reporting exceed what a spreadsheet handles well. A DBMS can enforce constraints, reduce redundancy, support multiple users, provide backup and recovery, and maintain a consistent source of truth. A spreadsheet is cheaper and familiar, but it is weak for scalability, access control, and data integrity in this scenario.

questions.question: Explain entities, relationships, attributes, cardinality, and optionality in an entity-relationship diagram.
questions.expected: Entities are objects or concepts being stored, such as Customer or Film. Attributes are properties of entities, such as customer name or screening time. Relationships connect entities, such as Customer books Ticket. Cardinality describes how many instances can participate, such as one-to-many or many-to-many. Optionality describes whether participation is required or optional.

questions.question: Name two inherent limitations of traditional TPSs and explain how ERP systems can overcome them.
questions.expected: One limitation is that TPSs are often siloed by business function, so data is not easily shared across departments. ERP addresses this through a centralized database and integrated modules. A second limitation is manual handoff between systems, where outputs from one TPS must be re-entered into another. ERP reduces this by allowing one transaction to update relevant modules automatically.

questions.question: Describe the main idea of ERP and name three typical ERP module areas.
questions.expected: ERP is a fully integrated, centralized information system spanning multiple functional areas of an organization, usually built around a shared database. Typical module areas include production and supply chain management, customer relationship management and sales ordering, and financial and managerial accounting. The purpose is consistent cross-functional data and coordinated workflows.

questions.question: Define a business process and explain why business processes often cross functional boundaries.
questions.expected: A business process is a collection of structured activities required to solve recurring business problems or produce value for customers. Processes often cross functional boundaries because work such as order fulfillment involves sales, inventory, finance, logistics, and customer service. Information systems must therefore support flows of material, information, and knowledge across departments.

questions.question: A digital product company is expanding internationally and has many customer interactions but little physical logistics. Which enterprise system is most important: CRM, SCM, or PLM? Explain.
questions.expected: CRM is most important because the company has a growing and diverse customer base and needs to manage customer encounters, sales, support, and repeat relationships. SCM is less central if there are few physical goods or logistics problems. PLM may matter for product development, but the scenario emphasizes customer relationship complexity rather than R&D coordination.

questions.question: Compare TPS, MIS, DSS, and ESS in terms of the decision level they support.
questions.expected: TPS supports daily operational transactions such as sales, payments, and inventory updates. MIS supports management monitoring and reporting about regular operations. DSS supports semi-structured or unstructured decisions using models, interaction, visualization, or what-if analysis. ESS is a specialized form of decision support for senior executives and strategic, long-term decisions.

questions.question: Explain when a DSS is more appropriate than an MIS report, using an example.
questions.expected: A DSS is more appropriate when the problem is semi-structured or unstructured and requires judgment, modeling, or scenario analysis. For example, deciding whether to enter a new international market requires assumptions, simulations, forecasts, and executive judgment, not only a scheduled sales report. An MIS report is better for routine monitoring of known indicators.

questions.question: Compare purchasing a software package, subscribing to SaaS, developing in-house, and using open source software.
questions.expected: Purchasing a package is fast and benefits from vendor development and upgrades, but customization is limited and lock-in can occur. SaaS has low upfront cost, very fast deployment, provider-managed updates, and scalability, but offers limited control and ongoing subscription dependence. In-house development fits unique requirements and builds internal capability, but is expensive and slow. Open source can be low cost and highly customizable, but support, integration, and community health are major concerns.

questions.question: Give three reasons why an organization might choose in-house development despite higher cost and longer deployment time.
questions.expected: An organization may choose in-house development when no commercial product satisfies unique requirements, when it wants to minimize changes to existing business processes, or when legacy-system constraints require a custom fit. It may also want to develop internal capabilities and maintain closer alignment between IT and operations. The trade-off is higher responsibility for maintenance, security, and scalability.

questions.question: Compare structured analysis, object-oriented analysis, and agile methods for requirements stability, user involvement, and complexity management.
questions.expected: Structured analysis works best when requirements are stable because it emphasizes upfront planning and sequential deliverables; user involvement is strongest early and users see the system late; complexity is managed through documentation and decomposition but changes are costly. Object-oriented analysis is more flexible because models and prototypes can be refined through cycles; users see prototypes earlier; complexity is managed through objects, encapsulation, and reusability. Agile is designed for changing requirements; it requires frequent user involvement through backlog refinement, sprint reviews, and feedback; complexity is managed by delivering small increments.

questions.question: Describe the main Scrum elements used in agile development and explain the output of a sprint.
questions.expected: Scrum uses a product backlog, sprint planning, daily Scrum meetings, sprint execution, and sprint review. During sprint planning, the team selects prioritized functionality to build in a short cycle. The output of a sprint should be working, tested, incrementally integrated functionality that can be demonstrated and potentially deployed.

questions.question: Explain the strengths and weaknesses of structured analysis for developing a new inventory management system.
questions.expected: Structured analysis provides clear phases, documentation, planning, and deliverables, which is useful if inventory requirements are stable and well understood. Its weakness is rigidity: changes discovered mid-project are costly, users may only see the system late, and it may struggle with complex or evolving requirements. It is best when predictability matters more than flexibility.

questions.question: A company needs a payment-service tool quickly but has strict compliance requirements. Explain the argument for SaaS and the main risks that must be checked before adoption.
questions.expected: SaaS is attractive because deployment is fast, upfront cost is low, scaling is handled by the provider, and updates are provider-managed. The company must check whether the provider meets compliance, data-protection, availability, audit, incident-response, integration, and data-export requirements. SaaS shifts operational burden but does not remove accountability for choosing and governing the provider.

questions.question: Name the four changeover strategies and compare them by risk and cost.
questions.expected: Direct changeover switches immediately from old to new and is fastest and cheapest, but has the highest risk and little rollback. Phased changeover rolls out by module, department, or stage, giving moderate risk and cost. Pilot changeover starts in one controlled area, reducing risk but increasing time and cost. Parallel changeover runs old and new systems simultaneously, giving the lowest risk but the highest cost and longest duration.

questions.question: Distinguish changeover from change management and explain why confusing them can harm implementation.
questions.expected: Changeover is the actual switch from the old system or process to the new one. Change management is the broader formal process of planning, communication, training, implementation, monitoring, and support. Confusing them is harmful because a technically successful switch can still fail if users are unprepared, communication is poor, or organizational disruption is not managed.

questions.question: Compare user training and user support in terms of timing, stance, and examples.
questions.expected: User training is proactive and equips users before, during, and sometimes after rollout through workshops, documentation, or e-learning. User support is reactive and helps users solve day-to-day issues on request through a help desk, knowledge base, or on-call IT. Both influence adoption and system utilization, but they serve different moments in the system lifecycle.

questions.question: Classify corrective, adaptive, perfective, and preventive maintenance and give an example of each.
questions.expected: Corrective maintenance fixes errors after the system goes live, such as patching a bug or security vulnerability. Adaptive maintenance modifies the system to fit a changed environment, such as new regulation or operating-system support. Perfective maintenance improves performance or usability, such as adding a requested feature or optimizing queries. Preventive maintenance reduces future risk, such as refactoring fragile code or replacing aging hardware.

questions.question: Compare ad-hoc and periodic systems reviews and explain why an organization should use both.
questions.expected: Ad-hoc reviews are event-driven, for example after incidents, breaches, major changes, or performance problems. Periodic reviews are scheduled, such as quarterly or annually, and provide regular oversight. Organizations need both because periodic reviews catch slow deterioration, while ad-hoc reviews respond to immediate risks and disruptions.

questions.question: Explain MTBF, MTTF, and MTTR and state what improvement direction is desirable for each.
questions.expected: MTBF means mean time between failures and measures availability; higher is better. MTTF means mean time to fail and measures reliability, especially for non-repairable systems; higher is better. MTTR means mean time to repair and measures maintainability; lower is better because the system is restored faster after failure.

questions.question: Define confidentiality, integrity, and availability and explain why security involves trade-offs.
questions.expected: Confidentiality means only authorized parties can access information. Integrity means only authorized parties can modify information. Availability means information is accessible for authorized use. Security involves trade-offs because a system open to everyone is unsafe, while a system locked down completely cannot be used; organizations must balance access and protection.

questions.question: Distinguish security policy, standard, guideline, procedure, and practice using the encryption example.
questions.expected: A policy states the mandatory goal, such as sensitive data must be encrypted. A standard gives mandatory measurable requirements, such as using AES-256. A guideline gives optional best-practice advice, such as preferring full-disk encryption on mobile devices. A procedure gives mandatory step-by-step instructions for configuring encryption. A practice describes what staff actually do in daily operations.

questions.question: Describe the four phases of risk management and explain how they lead to risk treatment.
questions.expected: Risk identification determines what risks exist and where they arise. Risk analysis evaluates likelihood and impact. Risk evaluation compares assessed risks with the organization's risk tolerance and prioritizes them. Risk treatment selects responses such as mitigation, avoidance, transfer, or acceptance. Monitoring and review should continue because risks and systems change over time.

questions.question: Compare mitigation, avoidance, transfer, and acceptance as risk treatment strategies.
questions.expected: Mitigation reduces likelihood or impact, such as adding MFA to reduce credential compromise. Avoidance eliminates the risky activity, such as discontinuing an obsolete system. Transfer moves responsibility or financial burden to another party, such as cyber insurance or outsourcing to a specialist provider. Acceptance means consciously tolerating a risk when further controls are not justified.

questions.question: Name the two stages of contingency planning and describe one activity associated with each stage.
questions.expected: The first stage is Business Impact Analysis, which prioritizes systems and processes for recovery planning by assessing the impact of downtime on revenue, delivery, reputation, and recovery criticality. The second stage is Incident Response Planning, which defines handling procedures before, during, and after incidents, such as backups, detection, containment, eradication, notification, recovery, and post-incident review.

questions.question: Explain RTO, RPO, MTD, and WRT and how they relate in recovery planning.
questions.expected: RTO is the target time to restore a system after failure. RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time, which determines backup frequency. MTD is the maximum tolerable downtime before unacceptable harm occurs. WRT is the time after technical restoration needed to resume normal operations. In planning, restoration plus work recovery should fit within the MTD, so the idea is $RTO + WRT \leq MTD$.

questions.question: Define security theater and explain why it is dangerous for organizations.
questions.expected: Security theater consists of countermeasures intended to provide feelings of improved security while doing little or nothing to actually improve security. It is dangerous because it misleads stakeholders into believing systems are protected while vulnerabilities remain, wastes resources, encourages compliance-box thinking, and can create user resistance or workarounds.

questions.question: Explain why strict password composition rules and mandatory periodic password changes can be security theater.
questions.expected: Strict composition rules often produce predictable patterns that attackers can enumerate, such as small variations on a base password. They also increase user friction, discourage password managers, and encourage reuse or written notes. Mandatory periodic changes can lead to predictable increments rather than stronger secrets. A better approach is long passwords, password managers, no unnecessary maximum length, and change only when compromise is suspected.

questions.question: Describe MFA and explain why the factors must come from different categories.
questions.expected: MFA requires authenticators from different categories: knowledge, possession, and inherence. The point is that compromise of one category, such as a password, should not be enough to authenticate. Two passwords are not true two-factor authentication because they are both knowledge factors; a password plus hardware key or biometric factor is stronger.

questions.question: Explain how rate limiting improves authentication security and name two trade-offs.
questions.expected: Rate limiting restricts repeated failed authentication attempts from a source such as an IP address, cookie, or account, making online guessing slower and more expensive. Trade-offs include accidental user lockout, account-lockout denial of service, and problems for users sharing an IP address. It is useful but must be calibrated carefully.

questions.question: Explain risk-based authentication and why it may be less theatrical than uniform user-facing friction.
questions.expected: Risk-based authentication evaluates contextual signals such as geolocation, device fingerprint, login time, and user-behavior patterns. Low-risk attempts may proceed normally, medium-risk attempts may require MFA, and high-risk attempts may be blocked or reviewed. It is less theatrical because friction is applied according to actual risk rather than making every user perform visible security tasks all the time.

questions.question: When can phishing simulations be useful, and when can they become security theater?
questions.expected: Phishing simulations can be useful when they measure resilience, create targeted teachable moments, and evaluate whether recent security measures work. They become theater when every employee receives generic blame-oriented tests regardless of role, when results are not connected to better controls, or when the organization substitutes user shaming for structural defenses such as MFA, filtering, reporting workflows, and incident response.

questions.question: Compare Westin's view of privacy with the Warren and Brandeis definition.
questions.expected: Warren and Brandeis describe privacy as the right to be left alone, emphasizing protection from intrusion. Westin defines privacy as the claim of individuals, groups, or institutions to determine when, how, and to what extent information about them is communicated to others. Westin is especially useful for information privacy because it focuses on control over personal information flows.

questions.question: Name Westin's four states of privacy and briefly explain each.
questions.expected: Solitude means being free from observation by others. Intimacy means private communication within a small trusted group. Anonymity means being able to act without identification or surveillance. Reserve means limiting disclosure and having others respect privacy boundaries.

questions.question: Explain how Solove's taxonomy makes privacy harms more concrete than a single abstract definition.
questions.expected: Solove's taxonomy breaks privacy into activities that cause harm, including information collection, information processing, information dissemination, and invasion. This helps analysis because a case can be classified as surveillance, aggregation, identification, secondary use, disclosure, exposure, intrusion, or another concrete harm. It avoids treating privacy as one vague value and instead identifies what went wrong.

questions.question: Explain the relationship between privacy, confidentiality, and security.
questions.expected: Confidentiality means only authorized parties can access information. Security protects data and systems from unauthorized access, modification, and disruption. Privacy concerns whether information disclosure or concealment is appropriate in context, so it goes beyond access control. Security can exist without privacy, such as in secure mass surveillance, but privacy cannot exist without security because insecure data cannot remain private.

questions.question: Explain the privacy paradox and provide an example involving personal information.
questions.expected: The privacy paradox is the attitude-behaviour gap where people state strong privacy concerns but do not behave in ways that protect privacy. For example, a person may say they worry about tracking but still use social-media or shopping apps with default location and profiling settings. The concept highlights a mismatch between stated concern and observable behaviour.

questions.question: Where does the privacy paradox fall short, and how does contextual integrity help resolve it?
questions.expected: The privacy paradox falls short because it assumes privacy attitudes are absolute and that users should always try to maximize protection. Contextual integrity argues that privacy is about appropriate information flows within a social context, considering actors, attributes, and transmission principles. Users may rationally share information in one context while objecting to a different use, such as social photos being used for facial-recognition training without consent.

questions.question: Define statistical disclosure control and explain its goal when publishing data.
questions.expected: Statistical disclosure control consists of statistical approaches to quantify and reduce identifiability in a dataset. Its goal is to release useful statistical or database information without revealing confidential information about respondents. It seeks a balance between privacy protection and analytical utility.

questions.question: Distinguish identifiers, quasi-identifiers, and sensitive attributes with examples.
questions.expected: Identifiers directly identify a person, such as name, passport number, or social security number. Quasi-identifiers do not directly identify alone but can identify in combination with other data or external information, such as ZIP code, date of birth, gender, or age. Sensitive attributes are values to protect from being linked to a person, such as disease, income, religion, or political opinion.

questions.question: Define $k$-anonymity and describe the basic procedure for achieving it.
questions.expected: $k$-anonymity means each individual in the dataset cannot be distinguished from at least $k - 1$ other individuals in the same equivalence class based on quasi-identifiers. The procedure is to remove direct identifiers, decide which attributes are quasi-identifiers, and then generalize, suppress, or code values until every quasi-identifier combination appears at least $k$ times. Higher $k$ improves protection against singling out but can reduce data utility.

questions.question: Explain homogeneity and background-knowledge attacks against $k$-anonymity.
questions.expected: A homogeneity attack occurs when all records in an equivalence class have the same sensitive value, so the attacker learns that value even without identifying the exact record. A background-knowledge attack occurs when the attacker combines quasi-identifiers with external information to narrow down which sensitive value applies to the target. These attacks show that $k$-anonymity protects against identity disclosure but not always sensitive-attribute disclosure.

questions.question: Define $l$-diversity and explain which weakness of $k$-anonymity it addresses.
questions.expected: $l$-diversity requires at least $l$ distinct sensitive values within each equivalence class. It addresses the homogeneity weakness of $k$-anonymity by ensuring that everyone in an equivalence class does not share the same sensitive attribute. However, it can still fail when sensitive values are semantically similar or heavily skewed.

questions.question: Define $t$-closeness and explain how it improves on $l$-diversity.
questions.expected: $t$-closeness requires the distribution of sensitive values in each equivalence class to be close to the distribution in the whole dataset, within threshold $t$. It can be expressed as $d(p_{z|x}(z|x), p_z(z)) \leq t$, where $d$ is a distance between distributions. It improves on $l$-diversity by addressing skewness and similarity problems, not just counting distinct sensitive values.

questions.question: A self-test asks you to compare ERP, CRM, SCM, and PLM in a short answer. What should a complete answer include?
questions.expected: A complete answer should define each system and connect it to a business need. ERP integrates core enterprise functions around a shared database. CRM manages customer encounters and relationships. SCM coordinates suppliers, production, and distribution. PLM supports product development from idea through retirement. The answer should also justify which system fits a given scenario rather than merely expanding the acronyms.

questions.question: A practice scenario describes employees using personal cloud storage to share company files outside IT oversight. Identify the concept and explain the main risk.
questions.expected: The concept is shadow IT, because employees are using technology resources outside formal IT-department oversight. The main risks are loss of security control, possible compliance violations, unmanaged access rights, weak monitoring, and difficulty ensuring that organizational data is stored, backed up, and deleted properly.

questions.question: For a self-test on post-implementation, list the four maintenance types and give the one-word purpose of each.
questions.expected: Corrective maintenance fixes faults. Adaptive maintenance adjusts the system to environmental or organizational changes. Perfective maintenance improves performance, usability, or functionality. Preventive maintenance avoids future problems. A good answer should also be able to attach an example to each type.

questions.question: A self-test dataset has groups of records where every quasi-identifier combination appears at least five times, but one group has only one disease value. Which privacy property is satisfied and which attack remains possible?
questions.expected: The dataset satisfies $5$-anonymity because each quasi-identifier combination appears at least five times. However, a homogeneity attack remains possible because all records in the equivalence class share the same sensitive disease value. The attacker can learn the sensitive attribute without needing to identify the exact record.

questions.question: A self-test asks whether mandatory password changes every 90 days are real security or security theater. What reasoning should the answer contain?
questions.expected: The answer should explain that mandatory periodic password changes can be security theater when they create visible effort without proportional risk reduction. Users often choose predictable variants, reuse passwords, or write them down. Stronger reasoning would mention long unique passwords, password managers, breach-triggered changes, MFA, and rate limiting as more risk-aligned controls.

questions.question: A self-test case has unstable requirements and highly available users. Which development approach is most suitable and why?
questions.expected: Agile is most suitable because it is designed for changing requirements and depends on frequent user involvement. The product backlog, sprint planning, sprint review, and incremental delivery let the team adjust priorities and learn from working software. Structured analysis would be weaker because late requirement changes are costly.

questions.question: Create a cram-sheet entry for the four risk treatment strategies with a short example for each.
questions.expected: Mitigate: reduce likelihood or impact, such as implementing MFA. Avoid: eliminate the risky activity, such as not storing sensitive data locally. Transfer: move financial or operational burden, such as cyber insurance or outsourcing. Accept: knowingly tolerate a low or justified risk without further controls.

questions.question: Write a concise cram-sheet contrast between changeover and change management.
questions.expected: Changeover is the actual switch from the old system to the new system. Change management is the broader formal process that plans, communicates, trains, implements, monitors, and supports the change. In short: changeover is the event; change management is the process that makes the event succeed.

questions.question: Produce a cram-sheet explanation of RTO, RPO, MTD, and WRT.
questions.expected: RTO is the target time to restore the system. RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time. MTD is the maximum downtime before unacceptable harm occurs. WRT is the time after restoration needed to fully resume normal work. A useful timeline relation is $RTO + WRT \leq MTD$.

questions.question: Write a cram-sheet contrast of $k$-anonymity, $l$-diversity, and $t$-closeness.
questions.expected: $k$-anonymity ensures each record is indistinguishable from at least $k - 1$ others on quasi-identifiers, reducing singling out. $l$-diversity requires at least $l$ distinct sensitive values per equivalence class, reducing homogeneity attacks. $t$-closeness requires each class's sensitive-value distribution to remain close to the whole dataset's distribution, reducing skewness and similarity attacks.

questions.question: Create a cram-sheet rule for choosing between package purchase, SaaS, in-house development, and open source.
questions.expected: Choose package purchase when requirements are common and fast implementation with vendor support matters. Choose SaaS when low upfront cost, fast deployment, scalability, and provider-managed updates matter more than customization. Choose in-house development when requirements are unique or legacy constraints are strong. Choose open source when low license cost and customizability matter, but the organization can handle support and integration.

questions.question: Write a cram-sheet entry explaining the privacy paradox and contextual integrity in exam-ready form.
questions.expected: The privacy paradox is the gap between stated privacy concern and actual disclosure behaviour. Its weakness is assuming privacy preferences are absolute. Contextual integrity resolves this by arguing that privacy depends on whether information flows are appropriate to the context, actors, attributes, and transmission principles. The same data sharing can be acceptable in one context and a violation in another.

questions.question: For an exam question asking to name two concepts, describe their role, and explain their connection, what answer structure should be used?
questions.expected: Use a repeated structure: concept name, role, connection. For example, state the component, define what it does, then explain how it interacts with other components or organizational processes. This prevents a list-only answer and directly matches the marking criteria for naming, description, and relationship.

questions.question: How should a student answer a scenario question asking which system or strategy is most appropriate?
questions.expected: The student should identify the best-fitting system or strategy, justify it using facts from the scenario, and mention at least one relevant trade-off. For example, choosing SaaS should be tied to fast deployment and low infrastructure responsibility, while also noting limited customization, provider dependence, or compliance checks. The answer should not merely define all options.

questions.question: An exam asks for three factors comparing structured analysis, object-oriented analysis, and agile. What makes the answer complete?
questions.expected: A complete answer names three comparison factors, such as requirements stability, user involvement, and complexity, and explains how each factor applies to all three approaches. The answer should not give a generic definition of each method only. It should show explicit comparison: structured analysis is sequential and documentation-heavy, object-oriented analysis is iterative with prototypes and objects, and agile is sprint-based with continuous feedback.

questions.question: What level of detail is appropriate for a short-answer exam response in this course?
questions.expected: The appropriate depth is concise but explanatory: name the concept, define or describe it, and connect it to the case or comparison. Model answers usually use two to five bullet-like statements per concept rather than long essays. A one-word label is insufficient, but a full theoretical discussion is usually unnecessary unless the question asks for it.

questions.question: Name three common exam traps in this course and explain how to avoid them.
questions.expected: One trap is confusing privacy, confidentiality, and security; avoid it by defining each separately. A second trap is treating security theater as any annoying security measure; avoid it by asking whether the measure actually reduces risk. A third trap is confusing changeover with change management; avoid it by remembering that changeover is the switch, while change management is the wider adoption process.

questions.question: Why are examples important in this course's written answers, and how should they be used?
questions.expected: Examples show that the student can apply concepts rather than only memorize definitions. They should be short, relevant, and tied to the concept being explained, such as using social-media tracking for the privacy paradox or financial systems for parallel changeover. The example should support the explanation, not replace it.
